item.title: “The four right efforts: Here, venerable sirs, a monk awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen…
item.description:
“The four right efforts: Here, venerable sirs, a monk awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states. He awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states. He awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states. He awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the continuance, non-disappearance, strengthening, increase, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 33 – Saṅgītisutta

item.title: “I do not see any other thing, monks, through which unarisen unwholesome states arise and arisen wholesome states decline, as heedlessness. For one who is…
item.description:
“I do not see any other thing, monks, through which unarisen unwholesome states arise and arisen wholesome states decline, as heedlessness. For one who is heedless, monks, unarisen unwholesome states arise and arisen wholesome states decline.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.58

item.title: “Venerable sir, thus a person has no stain but does not truly know: ‘There is no stain in me.’ For such a person, it can…
item.description:
“Venerable sir, thus a person has no stain but does not truly know: ‘There is no stain in me.’ For such a person, it can be expected: ‘He will attend to the sign of the beautiful. By attending to the sign of the beautiful, greed will pollute his mind. He will die with greed, with ill-will, with delusion, with stain, his mind polluted.’”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 5 – Anaṅgaṇasutta

item.title: “Monks, what is Right Intention? Intention of renunciation, intention of non-ill-will, intention of harmlessness. Monks, this is called Right Intention.”
item.description:
“Monks, what is Right Intention? Intention of renunciation, intention of non-ill-will, intention of harmlessness. Monks, this is called Right Intention.”

item.title: “Knowing this body to be like foam, Realizing its mirage-like nature, Breaking Māra’s flower-tipped arrows, One goes beyond the sight of the King of Death.”…
item.description:
“Knowing this body to be like foam,
Realizing its mirage-like nature,
Breaking Māra’s flower-tipped arrows,
One goes beyond the sight of the King of Death.”

“He who gathers flowers of sensual pleasures,
With mind attached, infatuated,
Death carries him away
As a flood sweeps away a sleeping village.”

“He who gathers flowers of sensual pleasures,
With mind attached, infatuated,
Before he has had his fill of sensual pleasures,
Is overpowered by death.”

From: Dhammapada 44-59

item.title: “Whatever things, monks, are unwholesome, partaking of the unwholesome, belonging to the unwholesome side — all of them have the mind as their forerunner. The…
item.description:
“Whatever things, monks, are unwholesome, partaking of the unwholesome, belonging to the unwholesome side — all of them have the mind as their forerunner. The mind arises first for those things, and the unwholesome states follow after.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.56

item.title: “Monks, just as a great tree, having its roots that extend downward and laterally, all those roots convey the sap upwards — that great tree,…
item.description:
“Monks, just as a great tree, having its roots that extend downward and laterally, all those roots convey the sap upwards — that great tree, being nourished and sustained in such a way, would stand for a long time. So too, monks, one who dwells seeing gratification in things that are clung to — craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging arises … Thus the origination of this whole mass of suffering. Monks, just as a great tree, and a man comes with a shovel and a basket. He cuts the tree’s roots … He digs a trench … he pulls out the rootlets … or he burns the tree and scatters the ashes in a strong stream of water. That great tree, with its roots cut, made like a palm stump, cannot be reborn, cannot arise again in the future. So too, monks, one who dwells seeing peril in things that are clung to — craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases … Thus the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.56

item.title: Another Elder Nun Dhīrā: Dhīrā, be steadfast, Hold fast to wholesome states. O nun, with faculties developed, Bear this last body, Having conquered the forces…
item.description:
Another Elder Nun Dhīrā:

Dhīrā, be steadfast,
Hold fast to wholesome states.
O nun, with faculties developed,
Bear this last body,
Having conquered the forces of Māra’s army,
Having conquered Māra with his army.

From: Therīgāthā 1.7
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, when form is born, subsists, arises, and becomes manifest — that is the birth of suffering, the subsisting of disease, the manifestation of aging…
item.description:
“Monks, when form is born, subsists, arises, and becomes manifest — that is the birth of suffering, the subsisting of disease, the manifestation of aging and death. When feeling … perception … formations … consciousness is born, subsists, arises, and becomes manifest — that is the birth of suffering, the subsisting of disease, the manifestation of aging and death. When form ceases, subsides, and passes away — that is the cessation of suffering, the subsiding of disease, the passing away of aging and death. When feeling … perception … formations … consciousness ceases, subsides, and passes away — that is the cessation of suffering, the subsiding of disease, the passing away of aging and death.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.30

item.title: “The mind is fickle and restless, Hard to guard, hard to restrain. The wise make it straight, Like a fletcher straightens an arrow.” “Like a…
item.description:
“The mind is fickle and restless,
Hard to guard, hard to restrain.
The wise make it straight,
Like a fletcher straightens an arrow.”

“Like a fish thrown on dry ground,
Wrenched from its watery home,
This mind struggles and thrashes
To escape Māra’s grip.”

“Hard to hold, fickle,
It jumps where it wishes.
Good is it to tame the mind —
A tamed mind brings happiness.”

“The mind is hard to see, subtle,
It jumps where it wishes.
The wise guard the mind —
A guarded mind brings happiness.”

From: Dhammapada 33-43
